# Exploring History

## The menu so far

Bucky has a few commits of history to work with:

```bash
git log --oneline
```

```
c3d4e5f (HEAD -> main) Add cheese curds and desserts
b2c3d4e Note how many brats to buy
a1b2c3d Add brats to the menu
```

<div class="gap-md"></div>

Your commit IDs will differ from these, and you may also see your cream-puffs commit from the last exercise — all expected.

<div class="gap-sm"></div>

History is only useful if you can [look back]{.uwred} at it and [recover]{.uwred} from mistakes. That is what this unit is about.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Bucky makes a change he'll regret

Late at night, Bucky second-guesses the whole plan. Open `brats.txt`:

```bash
nano brats.txt
```

<div class="gap-sm"></div>

Add a regrettable third line, then save and exit:

```
Bratwurst - simmer in beer and onions, then grill
Count: 2 per person (Bucky eats 4)
Swap the brats for a kale salad
```

<div class="gap-sm"></div>

In the cold light of game day, this was a mistake. We want the old `brats.txt` back.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## HEAD points to your latest commit

[HEAD]{.uwred} is Git's name for the commit you are currently on — normally your most recent one.

<div class="gap-sm"></div>

You can count backward from it:

- [`HEAD`]{.uwred} — the latest commit
- [`HEAD~1`]{.uwred} — one commit before that
- [`HEAD~2`]{.uwred} — two commits before that

<div class="gap-md"></div>

[`HEAD~1`]{.uwred}, [`HEAD~2`]{.uwred}, ... are easy for recent commits. To reach a specific commit further back, copy its [ID]{.uwred} from `git log --oneline` rather than counting.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Review before you restore

Good practice: look at what you are about to throw away. Compare your file to the last commit:

```bash
git diff HEAD brats.txt
```

<pre><code><strong>diff --git a/brats.txt b/brats.txt
index f735c2d..a9c3e21 100644
--- a/brats.txt
+++ b/brats.txt</strong>
<span style="color:teal;">@@ -1,2 +1,3 @@</span>
 Bratwurst - simmer in beer and onions, then grill
 Count: 2 per person (Bucky eats 4)
<span style="color:forestgreen;">+Swap the brats for a kale salad</span>
</code></pre>

<div class="gap-sm"></div>

The only difference from the last commit is the one regrettable line. Safe to discard.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Undo an uncommitted change: `git restore`

Throw away the edit and bring back the committed version:

```bash
git restore brats.txt
```

<div class="gap-sm"></div>

`git restore` prints nothing on success. Check the result:

```bash
cat brats.txt
```

```
Bratwurst - simmer in beer and onions, then grill
Count: 2 per person (Bucky eats 4)
```

<div class="gap-sm"></div>

The kale line is gone, and `git status` reports a clean working tree again.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## How `git restore` picks what to bring back

`git restore` reads a file from a [source]{.uwred} and writes it into your working directory.

<div class="gap-sm"></div>

- By default the source is the [staging area]{.uwred} — which matches your last commit unless you have staged something. That is what just undid the uncommitted edit.
- Point it at any commit with [`--source`]{.uwred} (short: `-s`) to reach back into history.

<div class="gap-md"></div>

It overwrites your current working copy with no undo, so [review with `git diff` first]{.uwred}.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Reach back to an older commit

Bucky is curious what the very first, one-line menu looked like. Find that commit's ID at the bottom of your log:

```bash
git log --oneline
```

```
...
a1b2c3d Add brats to the menu
```

<div class="gap-sm"></div>

Restore `brats.txt` from that commit — use your own ID (here, `a1b2c3d`):

```bash
git restore --source=a1b2c3d brats.txt
```

```bash
cat brats.txt
```

```
Bratwurst - simmer in beer and onions, then grill
```

<div class="gap-sm"></div>

Only the working copy changed; the staging area and history are untouched.


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## The older version is now an unstaged change

Because the working copy no longer matches the last commit, Git flags it as modified:

```bash
git status
```

```
On branch main
Changes not staged for commit:
  (use "git add <file>..." to update what will be committed)
  (use "git restore <file>..." to discard changes in working directory)
	modified:   brats.txt

no changes added to commit (use "git add" and/or "git commit -a")
```

<div class="gap-sm"></div>

Two choices from here:

- [Keep it]{.uwred}: `git add` + `git commit` to make the old version the new latest
- [Change your mind]{.uwred}: `git restore brats.txt` snaps back to `HEAD`

<div class="gap-md"></div>

So we all stay in sync for the rest of the lecture, let's all [snap back to `HEAD`]{.uwred}:

```bash
git restore brats.txt
```


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Try it
1. Add a silly line to `cheese_curds.txt` with `nano`
2. Preview it with `git diff HEAD cheese_curds.txt`
3. Discard it with `git restore cheese_curds.txt`
4. Peek at the original brats: copy the `Add brats to the menu` ID from `git log --oneline`, run `git restore --source=<that ID> brats.txt`, `cat` it, then `git restore brats.txt` to return to the latest
:::
:::


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Where we are

We can now travel through our history:

- [`HEAD`]{.uwred}, [`HEAD~1`]{.uwred}, ... name past commits
- [`git diff HEAD <file>`]{.uwred} reviews changes since the last commit
- [`git restore <file>`]{.uwred} discards uncommitted edits (from the staging area)
- [`git restore --source=<commit> <file>`]{.uwred} brings back an older version
